passage:
At 11 p.m., the engineering hostel's common room was empty except for Hansa and an old harmonium someone had left behind.
Her roommate Indu found her there. “Thermodynamics quiz tomorrow, Hansa.”
“I know. I've done it. Mostly.” Hansa's fingers kept moving over the keys, soft, so the warden wouldn't hear.
“You never play like this in the lab,” Indu said.
Hansa laughed. “The lab pays the rent later. This…” She stopped. “Papa says engineers never go hungry. He's right. I want that too. A steady salary, a flat for Amma.”
“And this?”
“This is the only hour of my day I don't check the clock.”
Indu sat down. “Both can be true, you know.”
Hansa nodded slowly. She did her circuits homework on time but with half her heart. The harmonium got the other half.

qa.q: What instrument did Hansa play in the common room?
qa.a: She played an old harmonium someone had left behind.

qa.q: How does Hansa feel about her two sets of reasons?
qa.a: She feels torn: she truly wants the security of an engineering salary for Amma, but only feels fully alive and free when she plays music.

qa.q: What could help Hansa bring more energy to both parts of her life?
qa.a: She could make regular time for music, such as a college music club, while talking with a mentor about how both goals might fit together.

qa.q: How does Indu see Hansa's situation?
qa.a: Indu sees that both motives are real and doesn't tell her to choose one, which may help Hansa feel less guilty.

grounding: The passage shows a student who chose engineering for security while drawn to music, with both motives real and her energy split between them.

passage:
Subject: Still playing (sort of)

Arohi Didi,

You asked how second year is going. Honestly? Two answers.

The first: I'm doing okay in civil engineering. I chose it because Papa's shop barely survived Covid, and I wanted a job nobody can take away. That reason is real. I still believe it.

The second: I miss the sitar more than I expected. I practise at 6 a.m., before labs, because that's the only time I feel like myself. On weekdays I drag myself to surveying; on Sundays I play for four hours without noticing.

I think that's why my grades are fine but not great. Part of me shows up to class, and part of me stays with the sitar.

I don't know how to fix it yet. Maybe I don't have to choose. Maybe I just need to stop pretending I only have one reason.

Nilesh

qa.a: Nilesh practises at 6 a.m., before labs.

qa.q: How does Nilesh feel about the two reasons in the letter?
qa.a: Nilesh feels torn: grateful for the security of engineering, yet longing for the sitar, which is the only time Nilesh feels like themself.

qa.q: What might help Nilesh, based on the letter?
qa.a: Stop pretending there is only one reason, and look for a way to keep both, such as regular music time alongside the course.

grounding: The email shows a student in engineering for security while drawn to music, and how the pull between both affects the energy brought to class.

So you're asking why I'm always half-asleep in mechanics, Baljeet. Fair question.
I'm Vikas. I picked mechanical engineering because my uncle said it's safe. Placements, a good salary, maybe a job abroad. And I want that. I watched my parents count every rupee. That's not nothing.
But here's the secret: every night I'm on the terrace with my guitar, writing songs until one o'clock. I've written twenty-three this year. I've written maybe two good lab reports.
When I'm writing a song, I forget to eat. When I'm doing a lab report, I check my phone every five minutes.
I'm not going to drop out. I also can't pretend the music is a hobby. Both of these are me. I just haven't figured out how to give each one a proper place yet.

qa.a: Vikas has written twenty-three songs this year.

qa.a: Vikas feels torn: genuinely wanting financial security, but absorbed and joyful only when writing songs.

passage:
Deepika, you're worried that little Kiaan asks “What will I get?” every time you ask him to help. Let me, your Tejas uncle, tell you what I did when I was your age.
I was twenty-five, a new father with a four-year-old called Neel. I'd started giving him a sticker for everything. Put away shoes, a sticker. Brush teeth, a sticker.
One day I asked him to help me water the plants and he said, “How many stickers?” and folded his arms. I felt a chill.
So I changed. I stopped the stickers, slowly. Instead I said things like, “You carried that heavy can all the way. The tulsi looks so happy now.”
It took weeks. But one morning Neel watered the plants before I woke. When I asked why, he said, “They were thirsty.”

qa.q: What did Neel ask when his father asked for help with the plants?
qa.a: He asked, “How many stickers?” and folded his arms.

qa.q: What did young Tejas feel when Neel asked about stickers?
qa.a: He felt a chill of worry, realising the rewards had replaced Neel's own reasons for helping.

qa.q: What choice did Tejas make in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: He slowly stopped the stickers and noticed Neel's effort and its meaning instead, which let the boy's own care return.

qa.q: How might Neel have felt when he watered the plants on his own?
qa.a: Neel probably felt proud and caring, helping because the plants were thirsty, not for a reward.

grounding: The elder's memory shows a young parent noticing his child asking about rewards before every chore and shifting to noticing effort and meaning.

passage:
Guests were arriving in an hour, the pressure cooker was hissing, and Nazia still had to clean the living room.
“Rukmini, can you put your blocks in the basket?”
Her five-year-old didn't move. “What will I get?”
Nazia stopped. That was the third time today. Crayons away: what will I get? Shoes on: what will I get? Since the chocolate-for-chores deal last month, every small task came with a price.
She knelt, even though the clock was ticking. “Nothing, today. But if the blocks are in the basket, Farah Aunty's baby won't trip on them.”
Rukmini thought about it. Then she started collecting blocks, slowly at first.
“That was really careful,” Nazia said. “You kept the tower pieces together.”
Rukmini beamed. She didn't mention chocolate. Nazia made a note in her head: fewer deals, more noticing.

qa.q: How long was it until the guests arrived?
qa.a: The guests were arriving in an hour.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when Rukmini asked for the third time?
qa.a: Nazia felt uneasy and a bit alarmed that the chocolate deal had made every chore come with a price.

qa.q: Which of Nazia's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Explaining the real reason, the baby tripping, and then noticing Rukmini's careful work; it gave the task meaning without a prize.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel when her mother praises her careful work?
qa.a: Rukmini seems proud and happy, enjoying being noticed more than the chocolate.

grounding: The passage shows a parent under time pressure noticing her child asks about a prize before every chore, and shifting to meaning and effort.

passage:
Saturday morning in the Irfan household meant a chore chart on the fridge, covered in gold stars. Six stars meant ice cream.
Irfan was folding laundry when he asked Ankita to fetch the socks from the balcony.
“How many stars?” she asked immediately.
He paused. “For bringing socks?”
“Yes. How many?”
Irfan looked at the chart. Every box was a transaction now. Last week she had refused to help Nani carry vegetables because “it's not on the chart.”
That night he took the chart down. The next morning, when Ankita set the table without being asked, he didn't give a star. He said, “You remembered Nani's spoon. That's thoughtful.”
Ankita looked at him, surprised, then smiled shyly. She went back and straightened the spoon.

qa.q: How many stars meant ice cream on the chart?
qa.a: Six stars meant ice cream.

qa.q: Why did Irfan pause when Ankita asked for stars for bringing socks?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and disappointed that every small task had become a transaction, especially after she refused to help Nani.

qa.q: What step did Irfan take, and why is it a wise one?
qa.a: He took the chart down and began noticing Ankita's thoughtfulness instead, so she helps because it matters, not for stars.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel when her father notices Nani's spoon?
qa.a: Ankita seems surprised and quietly proud, feeling seen for being thoughtful.

grounding: The passage shows a young father noticing his daughter asks about stars before every chore, and shifting to noticing effort and meaning.

passage:
Chetan's job at the insurance office in Nagpur was data entry. Claim forms, eight hours a day, nine to six. He'd taken it for the salary; his family needed it.
By the third month he was staring at the screen and typing like a machine. He barely remembered anything he entered.
One lunch hour, his colleague Arnab mentioned that the claims team used his entries to release payments. “That one you did yesterday? A farmer's tractor claim. Paid out this morning. His son rang to say thanks.”
Chetan thought about it all afternoon. The forms weren't just boxes. Somewhere, people were waiting.
He also started a small side goal: learning spreadsheet formulas to check his own entries.
The job was still dull. The salary still mattered most. But the afternoons felt steadier. He made fewer mistakes, and he minded the clock a little less.

qa.q: What happened to the farmer's tractor claim Chetan entered?
qa.a: It was paid out that morning, and the farmer's son rang to say thanks.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel after Arnab's story?
qa.a: He felt more connected and steadier, since his work mattered to people waiting for payments.

qa.q: What countermeasure did Chetan use against joyless work?
qa.a: He linked the task to people he cares about helping and set a small skill goal, learning spreadsheet formulas.

qa.q: How might Arnab see the change in Chetan?
qa.a: Arnab might notice Chetan seems less bored and more careful, and feel glad his lunchtime story helped.

grounding: The passage shows an adult in a dull paid job finding the part that connects to something valued and a skill being built, steadying effort.

passage:
“You look like a ghost, Tenzin.”
“I translated forty pages of washing-machine manual today, Zubin. Forty.”
“Riveting.”
“I only took it for the money. Rent's due.”
“So quit?”
“I can't quit. That's the point.” Tenzin rubbed her eyes. “I just feel like a photocopier.”
“Okay. Is there anything in it you care about? Even one thing?”
She thought. “Well… the Tibetan version goes to families in Dharamshala who've never had a manual in their language. My ama never read the English ones. She broke two machines.”
Zubin grinned. “So you're the reason someone's ama won't break a machine.”
Tenzin laughed despite herself. “And I'm getting faster with technical words. I might pitch for medical translation next year.”
“There you go.”
“It's still boring.”
“Sure. But now it's boring with a reason.”

qa.q: How many pages had Tenzin translated that day?
qa.a: She had translated forty pages of washing-machine manual.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel before Zubin's question, and what changed?
qa.a: She felt drained and bored, like a photocopier; after remembering the families and her ama, she felt a little lighter and more purposeful.

qa.q: What approach helped Tenzin, and why?
qa.a: Finding the part she values, helping families read manuals in their own language, and the skill she is building; it doesn't replace pay but steadies effort.

qa.q: How does Zubin see Tenzin's job?
qa.a: Zubin sees that it can be boring and meaningful at once, and helps her find the meaning without dismissing the boredom.

grounding: The dialogue shows an adult in a joyless paid task reconnecting it to something she values and a skill she is building.

passage:
For the first six months at the publishing house, I proofread Class 3 science textbooks and felt my brain turn to paste. Commas, captions, page numbers. I'm Arohi; I'd studied literature, and this was not the plan. The plan was the salary.
My colleague Nikita said something one evening that stuck. She said, “You know these books go to eleven lakh children, right? One wrong label and a kid in some village learns the heart is on the right.”
I started reading each page as if I were nine. Would this confuse me? Would this bore me?
I also began keeping notes on which layouts worked. It's turned into a skill: our editor now asks me to review new designs.
The work is still mostly commas. But when I sit down each morning, I'm not only thinking about my salary. I'm thinking of a nine-year-old with the book open.

qa.a: Nikita says they go to eleven lakh children.

“Lakshmi, sandals, quick. Let me.”
“No! I do it!” Lakshmi sat on the wet step and pushed her foot in. Wrong foot. She took it out and tried again. The auto driver tooted.
Amma breathed in and out. Then she held the umbrella over Lakshmi and waited.
Left sandal. Right sandal. One strap stuck. Lakshmi pulled it with both hands, face scrunched.
Click.
“Done!” She jumped up, splashing a puddle, and grabbed Amma's hand, grinning.

“Darshan, we'll miss the aarti! Give me your foot.”

He pushed his toes in. The heel folded. He pulled it out. Tried again. His lip wobbled, but when Chacha reached down, Darshan turned his whole body away.
Chacha sat on the step and waited.
Finally, both shoes were on. The laces were loose, but on. Darshan stood up very straight and marched to the door. “Now we go.”

passage:
Bidisha, you asked how I ever got through homework as a girl. Let me, your Nandini Dida, tell you.
I was ten, in Shillong, and I hated homework. Every evening my mother said, “Sit. Now.” And every evening I cried and sulked and did nothing.
Then one day she changed. She said, “You can do homework at five, before the radio programme, or at six-thirty, after it. You choose. And you can pick which subject first.”
I remember feeling suddenly grown-up. I chose six-thirty, and maths first, because I wanted it gone.
And I did it. Not happily every day, but without the war.
That small choice made me feel it was my homework, not hers. The work was the same. I was different.

qa.q: What were the two times young Nandini could choose?
qa.a: Five o'clock, before the radio programme, or six-thirty, after it.

qa.q: How did young Nandini feel when her mother offered the choice?
qa.a: She felt suddenly grown-up and trusted, as if the homework belonged to her.

qa.q: At what point in the story did the mother's choice change things?
qa.a: When she stopped saying “Sit. Now” and offered two times and which subject first, the daily fights ended.

qa.q: How might Nandini's mother have felt when the crying stopped?
qa.a: Her mother likely felt relieved and pleased that a small choice worked better than orders.

grounding: The grandmother's memory shows a parent letting a child choose between two study times and which subject first, which increased cooperation.

passage:
The power had gone in the whole colony, the inverter was beeping, and Kavitha had exactly one hour of light before the battery died. Vikas, nine, had a Hindi test and a maths worksheet.
“Vikas, homework. Now.”
He flopped on the sofa. “No.”
Kavitha opened her mouth to shout, then stopped. The battery beeped again.
“Okay,” she said. “Hindi first or maths first? You choose.”
Vikas sat up a little. “Maths. It's shorter.”
“And do you want to sit at the table or on the floor by the window?”
“Floor.”
She handed him the torch as backup. He worked for forty minutes without a single complaint, pencil moving fast. When the inverter finally died, he was on the last sum.
“Done,” he said, and looked almost pleased with himself.

qa.q: How long did Kavitha have before the inverter battery died?
qa.a: She had exactly one hour of light.

qa.q: Why did Vikas sit up a little when his mother asked which subject first?
qa.a: He felt more in control and respected, like the homework was partly his decision.

qa.q: Which approach worked for Kavitha, and why?
qa.a: Offering two small real choices, subject order and where to sit, which made Vikas feel like an agent and led him to cooperate.

qa.q: What might have happened if Kavitha had kept shouting?
qa.a: Vikas might have dug in and sulked, wasting the hour of light in an argument.

grounding: The passage shows a parent under pressure giving a child small real choices about homework, which increases his cooperation.

passage:
Every Sunday in their Chennai flat was the same fight. Minakshi's mother, Gopika, wanted the weekly revision done. Minakshi, eleven, wanted to do anything else.
This Sunday, Gopika tried something new. She wrote two times on a slip: “11 a.m.” and “4 p.m.” Then three subjects: science, Tamil, social.
“Pick a time. And pick the order.”
Minakshi squinted at the slip, suspicious. “Really? Any order?”
“Any order. But all three, and at the time you pick.”
Minakshi chose 4 p.m., social first. At 3:58 she came to the table on her own, carrying her books.
Gopika said nothing, just put a glass of buttermilk next to her.
Minakshi worked for an hour and a half. Afterwards she said, “Can I choose again next week?”

qa.q: What two times did Gopika write on the slip?
qa.a: She wrote “11 a.m.” and “4 p.m.”

qa.q: Why did Minakshi come to the table on her own at 3:58?

qa.a: Offering a choice of time and subject order within firm limits, so Minakshi felt like an agent.

passage:
“Anjali, wake up. Six-thirty: shower. Seven: breakfast. Seven-fifteen: revise chemistry. Eight: bus.”
“Mumma, I know.”
“Four: swimming. Six: tuition. Nine: bed.”

passage:
The summer I was fifteen, Sarita Masi came to stay, and suddenly there was a plan for everything.
“Kishore, you'll do physics till eleven. Then help me with lunch. Then an hour of reading. Then the cricket camp at five, I've already paid.”
I had wanted that cricket camp for two years. I'd shown Ma the brochure a dozen times.
But when Masi said “I've already paid,” something in me went hard. “I'm not going,” I said.
Ma looked shocked. So did I, a little. I stayed home at five, lying on my bed, furious and bored.
Looking back, it wasn't cricket I was refusing. It was the feeling of being moved around like a chess piece.
The next week I told Masi I'd make my own timetable. I put cricket on it, at five. I went every day.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 10, Tuesday.
Harsha's mother, Mrs Gopika Rao, came in concerned: Harsha has stopped doing anything she suggests, including the art class Harsha asked for in June. She showed me the family's shared calendar, with every half hour colour-coded by her, including “free time: 7:30–8.”
I met Harsha after lunch. Harsha was polite but tense, arms crossed. When I asked about art, Harsha said, “I did want it. Now it's just another box on Mumma's calendar.” When I asked what Harsha would choose if nobody was watching, the answer came quickly: art, and a walk alone.
My sense is that the refusals are protecting a feeling of ownership more than rejecting the tasks.
Next steps: I suggested to Mrs Rao that Harsha plan two evenings a week without her input, and that they agree on a few non-negotiables together. We will all meet again in two weeks.

passage:
You asked how I kept going in nursing when half my batch dropped out, Zainab. Let me tell you.
I'm Gurleen. In Class 12 everyone expected me to do engineering. I spent that whole summer volunteering at the Civil Hospital in Ludhiana, just to see. I sat with old patients, held hands during dressings, watched the nurses work double shifts.
Then I chose nursing. Not because I was told to. Because I'd seen it, the hard parts too.
Second year was brutal. Night duties, a patient I'd grown fond of died, and I failed pharmacology the first time.
My friend Tanu, who was pushed into it by her parents, quit that year. I understood why.
But every time I wanted to stop, I'd remember that summer. I chose this with my eyes open. That kept me standing. I passed pharmacology on the second go.

qa.q: Where did Gurleen volunteer the summer after Class 12?
qa.a: Gurleen volunteered at the Civil Hospital in Ludhiana.

qa.q: What kept Gurleen going when Gurleen felt like stopping?
qa.a: Gurleen felt steadier remembering that the choice was made with open eyes after seeing the hard parts, so the goal felt truly owned.

qa.q: What does Gurleen's story suggest about choosing a course?
qa.a: Taking time to see the real work before choosing, as Gurleen did, can build a commitment that holds through setbacks.

qa.q: How might Tanu have felt in the same brutal second year?
qa.a: Tanu, pushed into it by her parents, probably felt trapped and exhausted, with no reason of her own to keep going.

grounding: The spoken account shows a young adult who chose nursing after real reflection sustaining effort through hardship better than a friend pushed into it.

passage:
June: Manoj picked agricultural science after a summer on his uncle's farm, testing soil and talking to farmers. His roommate Kashish was there because his father owned a fertiliser shop and had filled in the form for him.
October: Their first field trial failed. Heavy rain rotted half the seedlings. Kashish threw his notebook on the bed. “Why am I even doing this?” Manoj was upset too, but he went back to the field at dawn and started recording what went wrong.
February: Kashish had missed most of the practicals and was talking about switching. Manoj had redone the trial with raised beds. It worked better. When his professor asked why he kept going after the rain, Manoj shrugged. “I wanted this before I got here. The rain didn't change that.”

qa.q: What happened to the first field trial in October?
qa.a: Heavy rain rotted half the seedlings.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel after the failed trial, and why did he return at dawn?

Bidisha, you're asking whether to take the architecture seat your parents want, or teaching, which you keep talking about. Let me, your Madhav Mama, tell you about two boys in 1996.
One was me. I was twenty and spent six months tutoring slum children in Howrah before deciding. I wanted to teach. My father sulked for a year.
The other was my friend Partha, who did chartered accountancy because his father said so.
In my third year the college almost shut down, we got no salary for four months during my internship, and I cried on the ferry more than once. But I'd seen those children's faces. I'd chosen it. I stayed.
Partha was brilliant, but when he failed a paper, he gave up. He said, “It was never mine anyway.”
I'm not telling you what to choose. I'm telling you: choose it yourself.

passage:
For eight months, my manager Deepak checked every single thing I did. Which font in the email. Whether I'd cc'd him. What time I called the vendor, and what I said. He'd rewrite my reports line by line.
At first I tried hard. Then I noticed I'd stopped trying. Why suggest a better supplier if he'd overrule it anyway? I started waiting for instructions, doing exactly what was asked, and logging off at six on the dot.
My energy went somewhere. I'm Yogesh, and I used to be the one who stayed late because I enjoyed it.
Then Deepak moved teams. The new manager said, “Here's what we need by Friday. How you get there is up to you.”
It took me two weeks to believe it. By the end of the month I'd found a vendor who saved us a lot. I stayed late one evening, and didn't mind.

qa.q: What did Deepak rewrite?
qa.a: He rewrote Yogesh's reports line by line.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh stop suggesting ideas?
qa.a: Yogesh felt drained and discouraged, since any idea would be overruled, so there seemed no point in taking initiative.

qa.q: What changed with the new manager, and why did it work?
qa.a: The new manager set a clear outcome and left the method to Yogesh, which gave room for judgement and brought initiative back.

qa.q: How might Deepak have seen his own checking?
qa.a: Deepak probably believed he was being careful and ensuring quality, without seeing it drain his team's energy.

grounding: The reflection shows a micromanaged worker losing energy and doing the minimum, and regaining initiative when given outcomes with freedom in method.

Department head's note, design studio, 2 May.
I have been observing Himani, a junior designer, for three weeks, after her work quality dropped.
Her team lead, Lavanya, reviews every file Himani touches, hourly. I watched one afternoon: Lavanya changed the colour of a button, then changed it back, then asked Himani to justify the spacing. Himani stopped offering her own layouts and began waiting to be told. At lunch she said to me, “I don't think anymore. I just do what's on the checklist.” She looked exhausted.
Lavanya is conscientious and means well, but the checking has taken away Himani's room to judge.
Next steps: I met both today. We agreed Lavanya will set clear outcomes for each project and review only at two checkpoints. Himani will choose her own approach in between. I will check with Himani in a month on how it feels.

qa.q: How often does Lavanya review Himani's files?
qa.a: Lavanya reviews every file Himani touches, hourly.

qa.q: How does Himani feel under the constant checking?
qa.a: She feels exhausted and discouraged, saying she doesn't think anymore and just follows the checklist.

qa.q: What did the department head arrange, and why could it help?
qa.a: Clear outcomes with only two review checkpoints, leaving Himani free to choose her approach, which should restore her initiative.

qa.q: How might Lavanya see her own reviewing?
qa.a: Lavanya probably sees it as being careful and responsible, not realising it is draining Himani's energy.

grounding: The department head's note shows a micromanaged junior losing initiative, and a plan of clear outcomes with freedom in method to restore it.

Thursday.
Francis messaged me eleven times today. “Did you start the report?” “Send me the outline first.” “Use my template, not yours.” “Why did you call the client without asking?”
I used to love this job. I'd come in with ideas. Today I realised I haven't suggested one thing in six weeks. What's the point? He'll redo it.
I did exactly what he said and left at 5:59. I felt nothing. Not proud, not annoyed. Just flat.
Tonight I wrote down what would help, so I don't lose it: tell me what you need and by when, then let me get there my way. Check at the end, not every hour.
Tomorrow I'm going to ask Francis for fifteen minutes and say it, calmly. My hands are sweating just writing that. But I'd rather feel nervous than feel nothing.
— Ira

qa.a: Francis messaged Ira eleven times today.

qa.q: How did Ira feel leaving at 5:59?
qa.a: Ira felt flat and empty, drained of the pride and energy the job used to bring.

qa.q: What does Ira want to ask Francis for, and why could it help?
qa.a: Clear outcomes and deadlines, with freedom in how to reach them and checks only at the end, which would give back room for judgement.

qa.q: How might Francis react when Ira asks for fifteen minutes?
qa.a: Francis might feel surprised or defensive at first, but could also be relieved to learn why Ira has become so quiet.

grounding: The diary shows a micromanaged worker's energy draining into doing the minimum, and naming clear outcomes with freedom in method as the fix.

It was Holi morning. The courtyard was wet and slippery with coloured water, and cousin Jagdish was shouting, “Careful, Simran!”
Simran, five, stood at the top of the three stone steps. For weeks she had jumped only from the lowest one.
She bent her knees. Jumped. Landed on both feet, splashing pink water everywhere.
She gasped. Then she laughed out loud.
“Again!” She ran back up. Jumped. Again. Again.
Jagdish gave up and just held out his hand at the bottom each time.
By the tenth jump, Simran was pink to the knees and grinning so hard her cheeks hurt.

qa.a: Jagdish probably felt worried about the slippery courtyard at first, then amused and happy for her.

Gargi's cousin's wedding was in four days, and the house was chaos: relatives on every mattress, a band practising next door, pressure cookers whistling.
Gargi, ten, sat in a corner with her fractions homework. Three-quarters plus one-half. She got 4/6. Wrong. She tried again. Wrong again. Yesterday's test had come back with a big red 3 out of 20.
Her brother Chinmay leaned over. “Common denominator, remember?”
“I don't remember. I never remember.” She shut the notebook. “I'm just stupid at maths.”
“You're not…”
“I am. Every time I try, it's wrong. So why try?”
She pushed the book under the mattress and went to watch the mehendi. Chinmay looked at the notebook, then at her, and didn't know what to say.

qa.a: She got 3 out of 20.

qa.a: She felt stupid and defeated after failing again and again, with no sense of getting better.

qa.q: How could someone help Gargi start feeling able again?
qa.a: A patient adult could sit with her in a quiet spot and work through very easy fraction steps, so she experiences small successes.

qa.a: Chinmay feels worried and helpless, wanting to comfort her but not knowing what to say.

Parveen's maths notebook was full of red crosses. Fractions. Again.
In the Lucknow tuition centre, Sumit Sir had drawn pizzas on the board. Everyone else nodded. Parveen stared. Why did two-eighths equal one-quarter? It didn't look equal.
She tried the first worksheet. Wrong. The second. Wrong. At the third, she stopped writing and drew a cat in the margin.
“Parveen, try question four,” Sumit Sir said.
“I can't do maths, Sir.” She said it calmly, as if it were a fact, like her name.
“You can learn this.”
“No. My brain isn't a maths brain. Ammi says she was bad at it too.”
She didn't open the worksheet again for the rest of the class. The red crosses stayed on the page.

qa.a: He had drawn pizzas on the board.

qa.a: After repeated failures she felt hopeless and defeated, and now believed it as a fact about herself, so trying felt pointless.

qa.a: Give her one very easy fraction she can get right, then build slowly, so she sees herself improving.

qa.a: Sumit Sir probably feels concerned and a little frustrated, wanting to help but finding her shut off.

“Lalremsiami, your homework?”
“I didn't do it, Papa.”
“Why?”
“Fractions.”
Amandeep sat beside her on the bed. “What about fractions?”
